_comment: Curated ANNOTATION for the repertoire bracket. Not the bracket itself.
The bracket — which slots exist, which branches a choice leaves open, how
often you face each one — is derived from master-tree.json and openings.json
by scripts/openings/build-repertoire-map.mjs. This file cannot make the
bracket wrong; it can only fail to improve it. That split is deliberate: a
hand-written repertoire tree would be stale the day after it was written and
nobody would be able to tell.
What curation adds: a human name, a sentence, the theory load, the kind of
position it leads to, and — the one load-bearing field — `family`, the ECO
name prefix used to PROVE which branches the choice absorbs.
coverage:
family  Absorption is proved against the named ECO family.
system  You play the same setup whatever they do, so there are no separate
branches to fill. ECO barely names system openings (the London has
6 named lines to the Caro-Kann's 103), so family matching would
invent gaps that are not real decisions.
move    Commits a move and nothing else. Correct for '1...e5': that is one
move, not a repertoire, and every White reply is still to decide.
Every `family` prefix is checked at build time and a miss FAILS the build.
A typo'd prefix matches nothing, which silently reads as 'this opening
covers none of its own theory' and fills the bracket with phantom gaps.
It has already happened once here, to a curly apostrophe.

`level` is the lowest band this is a sensible choice for; `load` is how much there is to memorise. They are SEPARATE axes on purpose. The King's Indian is heavy and beginner-suitable at the same time, because it has enormous theory and exactly one plan, and a single 'difficulty' number cannot say that.

choices.name: 1.e4
choices.blurb: The most played move in chess. You get open positions and fast development, and you answer whatever Black chooses.
choices.why: Positions open early and tactics decide the game, which is what actually wins points below 1200. Its cost is breadth, not depth: you will need an answer to six different defences.

choices.name: 1.d4
choices.blurb: Slower and more structural. Fewer forcing lines to memorise than 1.e4, and you keep a space edge for longer.
choices.why: Fewer forcing lines than 1.e4 and less to know by move five, at the price of slower positions where plans matter more than tricks.

choices.name: London System
choices.blurb: The same setup against almost anything Black plays. The least theory of any serious first move, and the reason it is everywhere below master level.
choices.why: One setup against almost everything Black does. The least to learn of any first move. It will also teach you less about the initiative than 1.e4 would, which is a real cost paid later.

choices.name: English Opening
choices.blurb: Flank play and a lot of transpositions. Rewards understanding structures over memorising lines.
choices.why: Transposes constantly, so it rewards knowing where lines GO rather than what the moves are. That is a skill built on top of an existing repertoire, not instead of one.

choices.name: Réti / 1.Nf3
choices.blurb: Keeps every option open and sidesteps most prepared defences by transposing later.
choices.why: Maximum flexibility, which only helps once you know what you are being flexible between.

choices.name: Nimzo-Larsen Attack
choices.blurb: Almost no theory and almost nobody prepares for it. You aim the bishop down the long diagonal and play chess.
choices.why: Almost no theory and almost nobody prepares for it. The structures are unusual, so you are relying on your own understanding from move three.

choices.name: Italian Game
choices.blurb: Natural development, an early bishop at Black's weakest square, and slow build-up or a quick d4 depending on taste.
choices.why: Natural development, a bishop aimed at the weakest square in Black's camp, and plans you can say out loud. The standard first opening for good reason.

choices.name: Ruy Lopez
choices.blurb: The deepest body of theory in chess and the most respected try for an edge. Expensive to learn, permanent once learned.
choices.why: Its whole value is depth, and depth only starts paying once opponents prepare against you. Before that you are memorising for an advantage nobody is contesting.

choices.name: Scotch Game
choices.blurb: Open the centre immediately. Far less theory than the Ruy Lopez and the play is concrete rather than manoeuvring.
choices.why: Opens the centre by move three, so the game is concrete rather than manoeuvring, and there is a fraction of the Ruy Lopez to memorise.

choices.name: Vienna Game
choices.blurb: A quiet-looking move that hides a very sharp f4 plan. Cheap to learn and rarely met with real preparation.
choices.why: Cheap to learn, much sharper than it looks, and almost never met with real preparation below club level.

choices.name: King's Gambit
choices.blurb: A pawn for the centre and the initiative. Objectively fine and practically terrifying to face without preparation.
choices.why: A pawn for the initiative. It wins a lot of games below 1200 and progressively fewer above it, which is worth knowing before you invest in it.

choices.name: Open Sicilian
choices.blurb: The critical test, and the most theory in the game: Black gets several systems and you need an answer to each.
choices.why: The most theory in chess, and Black chooses which of it you get. A bad bargain until you are meeting prepared opponents.

choices.name: Alapin
choices.blurb: Build the big centre and refuse the whole Open Sicilian argument. One system covers every Sicilian Black plays.
choices.why: One system against every Sicilian Black plays. The single biggest theory saving available to a 1.e4 player.

choices.name: Closed Sicilian
choices.blurb: A setup rather than a line: g3, Bg2, f4 and a kingside attack, with almost nothing to memorise.
choices.why: You set the pieces up the same way whatever Black does, so the whole Sicilian becomes one thing to learn instead of five.

choices.name: Rossolimo
choices.blurb: Meet 2...Nc6 with an early Bb5. A fraction of the Open Sicilian's theory for a real, lasting pull. It does not answer 2...d6, which is a separate decision.
choices.why: Real positional pull for a fraction of the Open Sicilian, but you have to understand the structures rather than follow moves.

choices.name: French: Advance
choices.blurb: Take the space and lock the centre. The plans repeat, which is why it costs so little to learn.
choices.why: Take the space, lock the centre, and play the same plan every game.

choices.name: French: Tarrasch
choices.blurb: 3.Nd2, sidestepping the Winawer entirely. Flexible and much less sharp than 3.Nc3.
choices.why: Sidesteps the Winawer entirely, at the price of quieter positions that need judgement rather than preparation.

choices.name: Caro-Kann: Advance
choices.blurb: Gain space and go after the bishop Black has just developed outside the pawn chain.
choices.why: One structure, reached by force, with a target to play against. Almost nothing to memorise and a plan that survives contact.

choices.name: Caro-Kann: Panov
choices.blurb: An isolated queen's pawn and open lines. Turns the most solid defence in chess into a fight.
choices.why: An isolated queen's pawn and open lines. Excellent training, and a structure that punishes drifting.

choices.name: Queen's Gambit
choices.blurb: The main line against 1...d5, and the most respected. Black gets several defences and each needs an answer.
choices.why: Every beginner book teaches this and they are right to: the ideas are the foundation of queen's pawn chess. Its cost is breadth, since Black has several defences.

choices.name: Catalan
choices.blurb: A fianchetto and a long squeeze. Positions repeat, so understanding compounds instead of expiring.
choices.why: The advantage is small and lasts fifty moves. That is only worth having if you are already converting small advantages, which is a club-level skill.

choices.name: Play c4 against the Indians
choices.blurb: The principled move. It also invites the Nimzo-Indian, King's Indian and Grünfeld, which are three separate answers.
choices.why: Principled and correct, and it hands Black the choice of three big defences. That is three separate preparations, which is a lot to owe at once.

choices.name: Trompowsky
choices.blurb: Second move, and Black's entire Indian preparation is already off the board.
choices.why: Two moves in and their preparation is gone. Almost nothing to learn and it works the same way against most of what Black tries.

choices.name: Sicilian: Najdorf
choices.blurb: The most analysed defence in chess and the most ambitious. You play for a win with Black, and you pay for it in study hours.
choices.why: The most analysed opening in chess. Below 1600 you will lose more games to not knowing move twelve than you will win from the extra chances.

choices.name: Sicilian: Dragon
choices.blurb: Opposite-side castling and a race. Whoever knows the line further usually wins, which cuts both ways.
choices.why: Both sides are attacking the same king with the same speed and the one who knows the line further wins. That is not a fair fight to walk into unprepared.

choices.name: Sicilian: Accelerated Dragon
choices.blurb: Dragon ideas at a fraction of the theory, at the cost of allowing the Maróczy bind.
choices.why: Dragon ideas at a fraction of the theory, at the price of allowing the Maróczy bind, which is a slow squeeze you have to know how to sit in.

choices.name: Sicilian: Kan
choices.blurb: Flexible and light on forced lines. You keep the structure fluid and decide what to be later.
choices.why: Few forced lines and a structure you commit to late. Easier to play than most Sicilians and harder to play well.

choices.name: 1...e5
choices.blurb: The classical reply. Be clear that it is one move and not a repertoire: White has six real tries and each needs its own answer.
choices.why: The best teacher there is: open positions, fast development, and every tactical pattern you need. Its cost is that White chooses which game you get.

choices.name: Caro-Kann Defence
choices.blurb: Solid, structurally sound, and unusually self-contained: it answers more of what White can throw at it than almost any other defence.
choices.why: Fewer separate decisions than any other answer to 1.e4, because it genuinely covers what White throws at it. That leaves you time for the rest of your chess.

choices.name: French Defence
choices.blurb: Give up some space, aim at d4, and accept a bad bishop you spend the game solving. Very consistent plans.
choices.why: The plans are the same in nearly every line, so what you learn in one game is still true in the next. That compounding is worth more early than any edge.

choices.name: Pirc Defence
choices.blurb: Let White build the centre and then hit it. Cheap in theory, demanding in understanding.
choices.why: Very little theory and a great deal of understanding. You let White build a big centre on purpose, which is easy to do badly.

choices.name: Scandinavian Defence
choices.blurb: You reach your structure by move three, every game. The least theory of any sound answer to 1.e4.
choices.why: You are in your own structure by move three, every single game, whatever White intended. Nothing else answers 1.e4 with so little to remember.

choices.name: Grünfeld Defence
choices.blurb: Invite the big centre and shoot at it from the side. Sharp, principled, and it leaves the whole 2.Bf4 / 2.Bg5 world unanswered.
choices.why: Sharp and principled, and it needs separate answers to 2.Bf4, 2.Bg5 and 2.Nc3 — a fifth of everything you will meet.

choices.name: King's Indian Defence
choices.blurb: Concede the centre, castle, and throw the kingside pawns at White's king. The most direct winning attempt against 1.d4.
choices.why: Enormous theory and exactly one plan: castle, play ...e5, and throw the kingside pawns at the king. You can play it on understanding for a long time before the theory starts to matter, which makes it far more forgiving than its reputation.

choices.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
choices.blurb: Pin the knight, trade it for structure, and play against the doubled pawns. The most respected answer to 1.d4.
choices.why: The trade-off is concrete but the timing is not, and mistiming it leaves you worse without anything obvious having gone wrong.

choices.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
choices.blurb: The old reliable. You will not be blown off the board, and the plans are the same every game.
choices.why: Nothing goes badly wrong in the first ten moves, which at this level is most of what an opening has to do.

choices.name: Slav Defence
choices.blurb: Hold the centre without shutting in the light-squared bishop, which is the one thing the QGD cannot do.
choices.why: Solid without the one problem the Queen's Gambit Declined has, and the plans are simple enough to hold in your head during a game.

choices.name: Dutch Defence
choices.blurb: An immediate kingside imbalance. Rare enough that most 1.d4 players have no prepared answer.
choices.why: You get an imbalance immediately, and you pay for it with a weakened king. Worth it once you can defend, expensive before then.

choices.name: Reversed Sicilian
choices.blurb: Meet the English by taking the centre yourself, with a tempo more than White has in the Sicilian.
choices.why: You are effectively playing a Sicilian a tempo up, which only helps if you already know what Sicilian players are trying to do.

choices.name: 1...Nf6 against the English
choices.blurb: Keep every option open and let White commit first. Often transposes straight into whatever you already play against 1.d4.
choices.why: Commits to nothing and usually transposes into whatever you already prepared for 1.d4, so it costs almost no extra work.

choices.name: 1...d5 against 1.Nf3
choices.blurb: Stake the centre at once. Most 1.Nf3 games transpose to a queen's pawn opening from here.
choices.why: One move, no theory, and most games become an ordinary queen's pawn opening you were preparing for anyway.

choices.name: 1...Nf6 against 1.Nf3
choices.blurb: The most flexible reply, and the one most likely to transpose into your existing 1.d4 defence.
choices.why: Keeps your options open and folds into your existing 1.d4 defence most of the time, so it is close to free.

choices.name: Tarrasch Defence
choices.blurb: Answer the Queen's Gambit by striking at the centre with ...c5 straight away, and accept an isolated queen's pawn for free piece play.
choices.why: One clear bargain: activity now against a weakness later. Easier to play than to play well, and it teaches you the isolated queen's pawn, which turns up everywhere.
